brief: A bite with USB in boots charger mode because the S2 reset type 7 (hard) power-cycles the PMIC and USB then counts as the power-on reason; the S2 type the firmware left (1, warm) is the one to try
found: READ, not measured on the bite: (1) Qualcomm: the PMIC records WHY it powered on in PON_REASON1 (KPDPWR_N, CBLPWR_N cable, USB_CHG, DC_CHG, hard-reset bit) and PON_ON_REASON separates a warm reset (0x40) from a normal power-on (0x80); the vendor says WARM_RESET is for crash dumps, HARD_RESET for restarting the device. (2) Our driver writes S2 type 0x07 (hard): the PMIC then powers its rails down and up like a cold start, so with the cable in the power-on reason is the cable (USB_CHG/CBLPWR_N), not a key press or a warm reset. A bootloader that sees a charger reason and no key press shows its off-mode charging screen: that matches the author's words (charging icon, black screen, Android only after a short power press). (3) The firmware had left S2 at type 0x01 (warm), read by the driver at probe ('S2 reset control was 0x1', booted 2026-11-20 run); mainline's own constants are 0x01 warm, 0x04 shutdown, 0x07 hard. A warm type keeps the PMIC peripherals on and sets the warm-reset bit, which bootloaders of this family read as 'not a cold boot' and do not send to the charger screen (the Qualcomm LK rule, recalled, NOT read: walleye's bootloader is closed and its rule is not confirmed here). (4) Android reported boot reason [reboot] after the later power press: that is Android's reading of the second boot, and says nothing of the bite's reason. NOT KNOWN YET: the PON_REASON/POFF/ON_REASON registers right after the bite (nobody read them before the second boot: the run read them only before arming); why z9 without patch 1 powered off while the firmware type was 1 (maybe the type was never read back there); what stock Android's own watchdog bite does on this phone (stock reset type). OPTIONS: A) arm S2 with warm type 0x01 (the firmware's own): smallest change, the series already has the reset-type hook; risk: the earlier z9 power-off; B) keep hard 0x07 and accept the charger screen when USB is in (the phone does restart; user-visible only with a cable); C) a PON bit or boot-reason handover before the bite (PON_SOFT_RB_SPARE as qcom-pon.c uses for reboot modes): works only if the bootloader reads it, unproven; D) leave it to the user space: nothing. LEAN: A, tried first because it is the firmware's own value, read-only experiment first (item walleye-wdt-bite-pon-reasons-read). Does not block the series: the bite proof stands.
question: Why does a PMIC-watchdog bite with USB in boot the bootloader's charger screen, and should the PON or the reset type make it warm-boot?

brief: A tool is followed by a pin, not files: device parts live beside it as data, hooks or a rust-script on the pinned library; rhizoid carries the cutting and slice cases and lacks three things.
found:
The question: a home for bring-up tools must also let device repositories use them, extend them with device-specific parts, send useful changes back and pull updates in, their own changes side by side with no rebase each time (the author's words, relayed by the coordinator; the problem git-rhizoid was started for). Extends research bringup-tools-landscape.
What is: the chain already decided (idealkb decision 2026-11-17-chain-follow-by-slice, research chain-follow-world): one pin-and-follow mechanism for data and briefs - a source names its generic files, a follower pins a release and keeps its own files, a changed generic file ends follow.sh with exit 3 and goes back as an upstream item (ikb upstream-item, form patch), weekly update-pins and a release gate; device bases follow idealkb and device-template that way. It lays a slice of files. Rhizoid (git-rhizoid.github.io, rhizoid repo) is for whole forks: a cutting is a fork owned and pinned, tracking branch pristine, patch branch merged from it, rhizoid's own metadata additive-only, so a diff of patch against tracking is a clean patch back; its CLI is typed but add/update/status are stubbed, its consumption side is open (design-consumption-side) and slice-consumption was added 2026-11-17 by the idealkb chain. devlab and lpoco-health already reach consumers as released packages (release-plz tags, the packaging conveyor), not as copied files.
Finding: a tool is not a slice. Compiled logic is followed by a version pin, not by files laid into the follower, so the rebase trouble does not arise for the tool at all as long as a device never edits the tool's tree: its own parts live in its own repository, beside the tool, in three levels. (1) Data: device.toml [boot] and the files it names (initramfs skeleton, dtb variants). (2) Hooks: executables the manifest names for a step (shell where stupid simple), called with the paths in arguments, a nonzero exit stops the job. (3) Logic: a rust-script file (or a small crate) in the device repository whose header depends on bringup's library at the pinned tag (rust-script and cargo take a git tag as a dependency). Only two things then need the follow machinery: the pin (a version line the follower owns) and the slice of files that go with the tool in device-template (the [boot] skeleton, hook examples). Sending back: a generic improvement is a pull request to lab-tools from the device's branch, recorded in the device base as an upstream item (form patch) against a lab-tools upstream row seeded beside idealkb and device-template; an update comes by a pin bump (the weekly job, a pull request per source). Side by side: the device's changes are files of its own, so a pin bump touches none of them; when a device must patch the tool itself before upstream takes it, that is a cutting of lab-tools consumed as a git dependency (Cargo [patch]) - rhizoid's exact case, rare because the three levels cover most.
Where rhizoid carries it, and what it lacks (recorded on its own backlog, git-rhizoid.github.io PR 28, not worked around): a cutting consumed by a language manager - writing and bumping the pin where cargo or rust-script reads it (cutting-as-cargo-dependency); one pin file, one bump, one verdict for slices, cuttings and tool versions together (followers-one-pin-bump); sending a patch back as a pull request on the person's word with the follower's own record of it (send-back-writes-the-upstream-item); and slice-consumption (already open) for the template files. Until rhizoid has them: idealkb's follow.sh and update-pins for the slices, a plain fork with a [patch] line for the rare cutting, recorded as a problem.
Not known yet: whether bringup's library API can stay stable enough for the third level while it is 0.x (the first builder's test of pin refusal tells); whether a host binary release (asset) or cargo install --git is the simpler install for a device lab (bringup-release settles it).
question: How do device repositories use, extend, send back to and update from a tools home, side by side with no rebase, and where does rhizoid fit?

brief: abootimg-oxide 0.5.2 writes the v0 header byte for byte as mkbootimg; the id (SHA-1 of three parts) and trailing padding are the caller's
found: Measured 2026-11-17 with a scratch program against mkbootimg (android-tools, header v0, base 0, kernel 0x8000, ramdisk 0x1000000, tags 0x100, page 4096): the crate's header write gave bytes identical to mkbootimg for the whole length it wrote. Two gaps, both ours to fill: (1) full_write only seeks to boot_image_size, so the image ends before the last page's padding (15288 of 16384 bytes) - pack pads itself; (2) the header id: mkbootimg's v0 id is SHA-1 over kernel, ramdisk and second, each followed by its u32 size (three parts), while the crate's compute_hash_digest hashes five (adds recovery dtbo and dtb) - so for v0 the id is computed in our code. With both, pack equals mkbootimg for the plain header and with os_version/os_patch_level words (tests/pack_v0.rs, two cases). mkbootimg writes second address 0 when there is no second image, whatever second_offset says. Header::parse reads v0..v2 and v3/v4; this tool reads v0 only for now. Cost: binrw and thiserror come with the crate. Not known yet: v1/v2 write parity, vendor_boot.
question: Does abootimg-oxide write header v0 byte-exact, or must pack wrap mkbootimg?

brief: No tool does build, swap and check of a boot image in Rust; the parts exist (header, cpio, dtb, compression) and the oracles are mkbootimg and avbtool, so we wrap.
found:
What is: walleye's bring-up is 8 POSIX shell scripts (~520 lines) in google-walleye-lab/build plus tests/host/gadget-up.sh; they call mkbootimg, unpack_bootimg and avbtool (Python from android-tools), the kernel's gen_init_cpio, lz4, fdtget/fdtdump, with their own checks (check-bootimg, check-bisect count fields and fail). Their knowledge is worth keeping: header v0 offsets by variant, the appended dtb, the lz4 frame shape of the stock kernel, the AVB hash footer (algorithm NONE, padded to the control's size), the NET=43 address rewrite, xz because the 4.4 kernel has no gzip. surya's bring-up had no scripts (by hand). Earlier records already decided the family: backlog rust-toolset (one Rust toolset in lab-tools, rust-script for small scripts, pmbootstrap read as reference) and decision 2026-11-17-health-checks-shell-and-rust (shell for plain readings, Rust for logic, rust-script for prototypes and one-offs).
Others: nothing covers the whole job. Android's mkbootimg/unpack_bootimg/repack_bootimg and avbtool (Python) are the authoritative oracles; magiskboot (Rust+C++, GPL) has the model of swapping one part (unpack to a directory, change, repack with the original as template) but is aimed at rooting; abootimg-oxide 0.5.2 (Rust, MIT/Apache, 2026-06) reads and writes header v0-v4 and vendor_boot; abootcrafter has an update flow, no AVB; abl-exorcist (Rust, GPL) shells out to mkbootimg; no AVB crate exists on crates.io (avbroot, GPL, does vbmeta, is no library). Rust crates for the rest: cpio 0.4.2 (newc writer), flate2, lz4_flex (maintained), dtoolkit 0.5.0 (Google, dtb read/edit, young), fdt (read). pmbootstrap is Python, ~24k lines in 129 files; its deviceinfo names (header_version, base, kernel_offset, ramdisk_offset, tags_offset, pagesize, cmdline) are the vocabulary to reuse; the boot image is not built there. Mobian, Droidian (initramfs-tools-halium: shell hooks for an initramfs only), lk2nd (a bootloader, no host tooling): nothing to take. No tool checks an image against expected header fields; unpack_bootimg plus a comparison is all there is, which is what our check scripts do.
Not known yet: whether abootimg-oxide writes byte-identical v0 images; dtoolkit's maturity; whether cpio 0.4.2 reads; whether boot-deploy, Mobian and Halium scripts add anything (not read; the outside look was done by a read-only researcher from page summaries, so counts are weaker than a source read).
Where tools live today: lab-tools (its README: tools for bringing up and testing Linux phones, not tied to one device) is the one place already: devlab (the phone: fastboot, flash, kernel try, provision, keeper, health, MCP; 5.4k lines with rmcp and tokio), health (runs on the phone) and tone. Device repos hold data and thin scripts.

brief: Images can be named by sha256 and made by recipe: Nix fixed-output paths are ensure; z21 rebuilt byte for byte by swap; hand-built kernels are not reproducible as recorded
found:
How it stands (2026-11-23). Images are declared by sha256 in device.toml [images.NAME] and booted by path from ~/Projects/walleye-build on one host; ~85 build/*.sh make them, mostly as an earlier image with parts swapped (a DAG rooted in a few hand-built kernels). lpoco-bringup already holds the deterministic steps in Rust (pack, swap, bisect series, initramfs build), but swap's AVB footer calls Python avbtool.
Measured: (1) lpoco bringup image swap z20 --dtb z21.dtb gives bdc0a891..., equal to [images.z21] sha256 - a recipe-shaped rebuild of an existing image, byte for byte. (2) Nix on the host stores an image as a fixed-output path computed from its sha256 and name; an unsigned file:// cache restores it for the normal user in 0.3 s, and a derivation whose outputHash is that sha256 then resolves without running its builder: Nix's fixed-output semantics are ensure. (3) An untrusted user cannot add a substituter (trusted-substituters empty): sharing goes by nix copy --from, or one nix.conf line for lab-machine's keeper. (4) The hand-built z20/z21 kernel cannot be rebuilt byte for byte from what was recorded: with timestamp, user, host, config and clang 23.1.5 set it still differed, by DTC_FLAGS=-@ in build-kernel.sh's environment, the built-in cpio's build moment and the build counter - all named knobs, none recorded.

found:
Measured 2026-11-17 on the kept kernel (7.1.0-sm7150-calls+, patched qcom_wdt), cycle 15 bt-on, as systemd-run units, nothing polled during a cycle.
(1) The DSP side, read awake: adsp, cdsp and modem remoteprocs running; qcom_stats adsp 0 (cdsp 56, modem 1798 counted): the three share one reader, so the layout is right for the subsystems; whether the ADSP firmware fills its own sleep-stats entry at all is not known yet. The only LPASS clocks enabled: LPASS_HW_MACRO (rx, tx macros and codec), TX_CORE_MCLK/NPL (rx, tx macros), fsgen - the macros' own clocks; the previous keeper's vote release did not change adsp.
(2) Others, read awake: genpd cx on at performance 256 with the two UARTs (88c000 Bluetooth, a88000) as devices; mx on 256; usb30_prim_gdsc on (USB gadget, the lab's link: qns_llcc/ebi avg 240000 peak 700000 are the USB's vote, cut by the cycle's gadget disconnect); ufs_phy_gdsc on; interconnect: only USB and the UARTs vote with bandwidth, the CPUs 8.7 GB/s peak; the PSCI cluster domain has states S0 (6 ms residency), S1 (8.5 ms) and S2 (9.8 ms): S2 entered once during the one cycle of that boot (s2idle count 1), so the cluster reached its deepest state.

Not known yet: which; this kernel has no RPMh trace points (events: clk, regulator, interconnect, power/psci_domain_idle_enter only).
Not measured: a cycle with the UARTs closed; the PSCI state taken at the suspend; the live rpmh sleep-set contents.

brief: The AOP's view is not readable from Linux; the flush is sound; peers on near-mainline never read the counters as good either, so standby current, not aosd, is the arbiter
found:
(1) Does the AOP get the flush. The entry trace already shows the Apps RSC writes wake and sleep sets in one instant on the last CPU and then requests the deepest cluster state (0x4100b244), so Linux's half is done in order. The AOP's half is not observable from Linux: the only outputs are the counters it fills (aosd, cxsd, ddr in the message RAM) and the rails. Nothing in mainline reads an AOP log. What the AOP needs for cxsd is every master's sleep vote on CX gone (Apps, modem, adsp, cdsp, display, WLAN BB), not only Apps'. A peer found exactly that kind of cause: on SM7325 a WLAN BB vote prevented CX power collapse (CXPC) and, once removed, "HLOS and DDR votes remain" (pmaports#4846, 2026-11-16); on SM8550 an SD-controller IRQ storm and a USB PHY vote did (armada#274). So the entry is not the open question any more; the other masters' votes and the wakeups are.

(2) Why the cluster genpd S2idle column stays 0. From core.c: usage_s2idle is incremented only in genpd_sync_power_off, after the domain's governor (pm_domain_cpu_gov, set by cpuidle-psci-domain only when the domain has idle states) approved the power-down, and that function returns early unless every device attached to the cluster domain has been suspended (suspended_count == device_count) and every child CPU domain is off. s2idle reaches it through dev_pm_genpd_suspend, not runtime PM. The trace shows the cluster bits in the PSCI state (0x4100b244), so the cluster power-off callback did run; then either the counter is read from the wrong row/domain, or the state composed is from a path that did not count. Both are cheap to tell apart and are not known yet: read idle_states of every power-domain-* after one cycle (all rows, all columns) and the psci_domain_idle_enter trace's s2idle flag.

(3) Is the SoC asleep already, and the arbiter. The peer record says the counters are not the whole picture: motorola-dubai (SM7325) reads S2 for ~1 ms, and the author of the qclaptops tree removed WLAN BB, touch, audio and regulator holders with "idle drain lowered by 0.00000 W". Standby current moved only with: USB runtime PM allowed (0.196 -> 0.180 W), the camera VCM and always-on audio regulators released, modem off. The same report measures current_now: near-mainline 152 mA (later 60 mA, 0.2-0.3 W), the same-era Droidian downstream kernel on xiaomi-miatoll (SM6250) 9 mA. So a number exists to match: about 9 mA average with screen off on a Snapdragon 6/7-series phone running the vendor kernel. Android's own number on surya is not known yet: nobody has measured it, and the public sources give no standby current (android-reference).

(4) Cheaper tools than the AOP: regulator_summary (what rails stay on, with users), pm_genpd_summary, qcom_stats, and current_now / charge_counter. Android's value is the end, regulators the where.
question: Does the AOP receive the RSC sleep flush, why is the cluster genpd S2idle column 0, and is the SoC perhaps already asleep - how does standby current arbitrate, and what is Android's to match?

brief: Counters look valid; SH0 is not shown to block (awake icc read is not the flush moment); the unread facts are the RSC flush, last-CPU idle state and IRQ rate at entry
found:
Question 1, counter validity: the counters are very probably valid. qcom_stats creates its files by reading each record's name word out of the message RAM (qcom_stats.c), and surya has aosd, cxsd and ddr: three names read, not assumed. ddr_stats also passed its magic key, and its frequency rows move while the LPM rows stay 0 (research floor-holders), so the block is live and the layout is the one sc7180 uses, where the Acer Aspire 1 counts. adsp 0 and empty apss/display/gpu are SMEM entries this firmware does not fill; they are not the SoC counters. Not found anywhere: an Android reading of these counters on SM7150 (no source, none observed). Only an independent measure can make the last doubt certain: standby current (sleep-standby-current).

Question 2, is SH0 x=1,y=3 the blocker: not shown, and the reading rests on a mix-up that is worth fixing. bcm-voter.c forces keepalive BCMs only in the AMC and WAKE buckets, so a SLEEP-bucket x=1,y=3 means some request with a SLEEP-bearing tag (ALWAYS = 7) had non-zero bandwidth at the flush. The awake icc summary is not that moment: the only large vote there is USB (240000 = USB_MEMORY_AVG_HS_BW in dwc3-qcom.c, tag 7) and dwc3_qcom_suspend sets it to 0 before the last CPU flushes; the peak is cpu0/cpu6 at tag 3 (AMC|WAKE, not SLEEP). So the vote that makes x=1,y=3 is one nobody has seen being made: not USB as a floor holder (UDC unbound: counters 0 -> 0; whether SH0 changed was not read), not uart8, not the cpufreq votes by tag. Two readings remain and they cannot be told apart by subtracting: (a) the flush the log shows is stale or not the last one, i.e. the sleep set is not what the AOP sees at entry; (b) SH0 is harmless and something else blocks. So SH0 is demoted from "the blocker" to "one unexplained entry"; no more owner-hunting by tag until the entry is read.

What is the blocker then: the three observations nobody has taken at the entry itself. (1) Is the RSC flush invoked on the last CPU and what does it write (tracepoints rpmh_send_msg state=sleep; rpmh_rsc_cpu_pm_callback flushes at CPU_PM_ENTER of the last online CPU). (2) What the last CPU's idle state is (power:cpu_idle with the PSCI state, per-CPU cpuidle usage/time deltas): a cycle can "take" the cluster state once and still wake every few ms. (3) Whether anything wakes the CPUs during the 15 s: /proc/interrupts delta. This last one is what the nearest measured sibling found: on the Odin 2 (SM8550) suspend succeeded, counters read 0, and the cause was an SD controller firing ~30 irq/s through the whole suspend plus a USB PHY vote and CPU0 idle disabled (armada#274). The Qualcomm guide's own order for "aosd count zero" is also: display off, USB disconnected, suspend success count, then wake locks. Surya has never had its interrupt rate read across a cycle; devlab-usb is also a wakeup source active the whole time (research floor-holders).

Question 3, what a late-suspend dump should read: per-CPU cpuidle state usage/time before and after; the cluster genpd idle_states usage (taken, rejected) and the time spent; the sleep-set commands written (trace rpmh); /proc/interrupts delta; wakeup_sources; suspend_stats; qcom_stats of all nodes before and after (including each subsystem's last-entered time). All of it is tracefs/procfs/debugfs: no kernel build is needed, so floor-suspend-late-dump (a debug kernel) is not first.
Also AOP QMP: the AOP does process RSC commands (regulators, rpmhpd and icc work), so it is alive; QMP is a separate channel and, as found, off the path.
Sources read, not run on the phone; nothing on the phone was touched.
question: Is SH0 x=1,y=3 the blocker at all - counter validity, clocks/GDSC, late-suspend state?

brief: The suspend wake is irq 158 (GPIO 41, the UART RX line, the serial's dedicated wake irq), not 157; the serial's power/wakeup is its mainline switch
found: Measured 2026-11-17 on 7.1.0-sm7150-calls+ with ftrace and a kprobe on pm_system_irq_wakeup (suspend-wake-arm-trace.sh in the material): s2idle was ended by irq 158 ('88c000.serial:wakeup', msmgpio 41, edge), armed by dev_pm_arm_wake_irq in the late phase because the platform device 88c000.serial has power/wakeup enabled (qcom_geni_serial sets device_init_wakeup and dev_pm_set_dedicated_wake_irq when the DT gives a second interrupt: the RX pin). The main irq 157 (GIC 636) fires 6 times at the end of qca_suspend, which waits up to 2 s for the chip's sleep indication (hci_qca.c); no 'nobody cared' appeared in these tries. Mainline source read (torvalds/linux master): uart_suspend_port keeps the irq wake only if the tty device serial0 may wakeup (here disabled); hci_qca qca_wakeup() returns device_may_wakeup of the serdev controller and the Bluetooth core then arms a passive scan for suspend, so an RX edge from the chip is a wake by design; the switch is the serial's power/wakeup, a plain sysfs file. With it off for a cycle, s2idle ends by the RTC alarm (RTC counted 7 s for 5 asked, 7 s for 5, 17 s for 15) with hci0 up and scanning after. brief: SH0 is a keepalive LLCC BCM; its sleep residual is a TAG_ALWAYS consumer (QUP/uart8), not a latch; AOP QMP wiring equals sm8150, no-ack unexplained
found:
SH0 is not a holder someone took; it is a keepalive BCM. In mainline sm7150.c, bcm_sh0 is "SH0", keepalive, node qns_llcc, identical to sdm845, sm8150 and sc7180 (the sc7180 Acer Aspire 1 reaches cxsd/aosd/ddr counts with the same definition). bcm-voter.c forces keepalive BCMs to x=y=1 (or enable_mask) only in the AMC and WAKE buckets. The SLEEP bucket is aggregated from consumers' tags only, so a sleep-set SH0 x=1,y=3 means a consumer whose tag includes SLEEP (QCOM_ICC_TAG_ALWAYS = AMC|WAKE|SLEEP) has a path through qns_llcc with a tiny bandwidth. In sm7150.dtsi the candidates are the QUP nodes, which use TAG_ALWAYS interconnects (one serial toward gem_noc SLAVE_LLCC, near line 1259), the crypto engine (ALWAYS to EBI, line 460), and uart8 serial@a88000 (the debug UART), which the recorded cycles show at avg 1 peak 1 across suspend. The owner is a DT tag on a consumer, not a firmware latch.
Whether the SH0 sleep vote blocks aosd is NOT known yet: no source shows the sleep-set contents of the Aspire 1 or any SM7150-class phone; SH0 is only the sole non-zero sleep entry on surya, which makes it the cheapest subtraction.
QMP: the aoss_qmp node (c300000, spi 389, mboxes apss_shared 0, apss_shared at 17c00000) is identical to sm8150 and sc7180, so the wiring in the tree is not the difference. Open succeeds, every send times out: the AOP does not clear the length word after the kick; qmp_send gives no other signal. Downstream wiring (irq-reg-base 17c0000c, mask 1) could not be confirmed from a source this session - not known yet. QMP matters only for the aoss prevent knobs (cx_mol, ddr_mol; hypothesis 5, unlikely) and is not on the path to the SH0 owner.
Read from the tree at kernel-rc3; nothing on the phone was touched.

brief: surya has the qcom_wdt watchdog, 4 MiB ramoops and a PMIC RTC (1970); the stock watchdog is stopped in late suspend, so no way back covers a hang inside s2idle
found: On the phone: qcom_wdt (17c10000.watchdog) with /dev/watchdog0, ramoops 4 MiB reserved at 0x9d800000 with pstore (console 1 MiB), the PMIC RTC reading 1970 and settable with hwclock -w -u; the kernel has no suspend timeout of its own (no PM_DEBUG, hung-task, DPM watchdog). Mainline qcom-wdt.c registers late system sleep ops that STOP an active watchdog in suspend and start it on resume: so a hang before the late phase is covered by a watchdog, one inside s2idle is not. A module with that stop made optional (one parameter, no other change) builds for the running kernel (no MODVERSIONS; vermagic equals uname -r) and loads without a kernel rebuild or reboot-to-test; a reboot undoes it. The RTC alarm cannot be the way back: if the RTC wake does not reach the GIC out of s2idle the phone sleeps for good, which looks the same as a hang. A bite resets the SoC; whether it reaches a normal boot and whether ramoops survives it is what the dry run measures.

brief: Surya's BT device tree already equals mainline's s2idle-capable sc7180 wiring (CTS bias aside); failures are sleep/SSR timeouts and a level irq storm; others fix it in user space
found: Read 2026-11-18. (1) Surya's device tree already is the mainline pattern: the live /sys/firmware/devicetree node serial@88c000 has interrupts-extended (GIC 604 + tlmm 41 edge falling), pinctrl default+sleep, bluetooth compatible qcom,wcn3998-bt. Its sleep state: CTS gpio38 bias-bus-hold, RTS gpio39 pull-down, TX gpio40 pull-up, RX gpio41 pull-up. The only mainline QCA UART Bluetooth built to sleep in s2idle, sc7180-trogdor (same GPIO 38-41, same qup03), has the same wiring; its sleep state differs in one pin: CTS gets bias-pull-down 'to match the pull of the Bluetooth module' (surya: bus-hold). So the DT is not what is missing; one pin bias is the only measured-nowhere difference. (2) Mechanism of the failures, from the code: qca_suspend waits only 200 ms for the chip's own HCI_IBS_SLEEP_IND and returns -ETIMEDOUT (suspend then refuses, as in r4 'qca_suspend returned -110'); during SSR it waits up to memdump+3 s then times out. qcom_geni_serial_isr returns IRQ_NONE while uport->suspended, and irq 157 is a level irq: any RX/CTS activity from the chip after the port is suspended, or while a crashed controller keeps talking, is the 'nobody cared' storm. Not measured: whether the storm comes before or after the controller crash (r4 shows both within 8 s, order unread). (3) What others do: mainline gives no hook - Chromebooks (trogdor) rely on in-band sleep plus the RX wake; every desktop/distro remedy found is user space: bluetoothctl power off before sleep (ArchWiki), rfkill block in a sleep hook (pop-os, which breaks BT peripherals and needs a power cycle), and for a QCA UART controller that loses state, unbinding only the serdev from hci_uart_qca before sleep and binding it after (SteamOS 2845, worked across S4). No postmarketOS/Mobian/Droidian rule for qca UART Bluetooth across s2idle was found in two searches (only our earlier note of a pmOS hook stopping Bluetooth for the Pixel 3a FastRPC crash); not found is not absent. (4) Local facts that bound the choice: wakeup off + BT up passed 4 of 4 15 s cycles (irq157-quiet-with-wakeup-off) yet r4 failed at its first long off-USB run; BT blocked (rfkill) hung suspend entry hard twice (surya-s2idle-bt-blocked-hang, sh0-bt-blocked-cycle-resets) - so closing the port is not safe; unbind and power-off by serdev remove were never tried; the r4 wedge was sxmo calling rtcwake in a 1-20 s loop while the controller sat in SSR, with three rfkill processes on the misc_open mutex, not a kernel panic. Ways it could go: A mirror trogdor exactly (CTS pull-down in sleep) and run with the wakeup switch on; B unbind hci_uart_qca (serdev) before suspend, bind after - a clean controller power-off and a full re-setup, never rfkill; C gate sxmo's autosleep on a healthy hci0 (no suspend while SSR or rfkill busy), which cannot fix the storm but removes the wedge; D take Bluetooth off the standby profile (bluetoothctl power off) - the ArchWiki remedy, loses BT peripherals; E patch hci_qca (longer sleep wait, reset on timeout) - upstream-shaped but needs the cause first.

brief: What made the TX decimator to codec DMA path deliver zeros, and what does a capture of zeros tell?
found: The decimator-to-DSP leg worked all along: each silent recording began with ~0.5 s of ringing (-1774 settling to exact 0), the high-pass filter draining a constant input - the decimator ran and its output reached TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3, but no samples entered it. The cause was upstream of the decimator: the capture link named the TX SoundWire controller's DAI 0, its playback DAI (qcom_swrm_register_dais makes the first num_dout_ports DAIs playback, and this controller has one dout port), so sdw_stream_add_master was never called and the codec's ports never programmed. The same one-dout-port shift moves master port numbers by one (ports start at 2; swr2's qcom,ports-* arrays begin with 0xff). For DMICs the same reading held: with no clock on the pin the data line is static and the filter removes it. So: start-up ringing then exact zeros means no input reaches the decimator - look at the source (SoundWire stream, DMIC clock), not the DMA or the AFE port. The AFE port is the vendor's too: TX AIF1 on TX_CDC_DMA_TX_3 (45111 = 0xB037), accepted by this ADSP.
question: What made the TX decimator to codec DMA path deliver zeros, and what does a capture of zeros tell?

brief: Why does nothing come back from surya's main microphone, now that the WCD9375 enumerates and the sound card is made?
found: The codec dropped off both SoundWire buses because ASoC puts every idle component into its sleep pin state, and the codec's sleep state drove its active-low reset low (traced: snd_soc_bind_card committed it 0.24 ms before both interfaces went UNATTACHED). Without a sleep state the codec stays attached and capture prepares (linux-phone-oco/linux PR #4); the SoundWire pin-mux fix is PR #3. Capture still yields exact zeros: the built-in microphones are digital mics (vendor: TX DMIC1-3 on LPI gpio26-29, function 1, mic bias 1 and 3); this ADSP rejects the VA capture port, so they go through the TX macro to TX_CODEC_DMA_TX_3; with the VA DMIC clocks forced on the TX path still reads zeros, as it does from ADC1 - the next fault sits in the TX decimator to DSP leg. Details: research/microphone.md.

The phone runs libssc 0.4.3 with ssccli, iio-sensor-proxy 3.9 with ssc support, and its udev tags fastrpc-adsp ssc-light, ssc-compass, ssc-accel, ssc-proximity; iio-sensor-proxy starts and waits ('registry sensor unavailable'). brief: Why does the ADSP sensors service crash-loop the audio DSP on surya, and what would stop it without changing the firmware?
found: Measured on the phone (read only, kept kernel 7.1.0-sm7150-calls+, 2026-11-17) and read in hexagonrpcd's source. At start the DSP's registry sensor compares each config it knows (the registry's sns_reg_config: 47 configs, every one recorded with data 1230768000 - 2009-01-01, Android's fixed vendor mtime) with the config files hexagonrpcd serves, and hexagonrpcd passes their real mtime: all 46 on the phone carry 1779945838 (the package's build time), and sns_pickup.json is listed but absent. Every config therefore looks changed, the DSP re-parses and writes (temp.json), hexagonrpcd refuses every write by design, and the DSP asserts (SNS_REG_INIT, sns_registry_sensor.c) and restarts with audio. The version marker sns_reg_version, whose absence also forces a rebuild elsewhere (hexagonrpc #19), cannot be served at all: the virtual persist/sensors/registry holds only its registry subdirectory. So no trial of 2026-11-09 had both conditions of an untouched registry - the marker reached and the configs unchanged; they disproved only a registry swap. Hypothesis to settle first: configs touched to 1230768000 (and no listed config missing) make the pre-parsed registry current, so nothing is written and the ADSP stays up. brief: Does sm7150's device tree ask the firmware for the cluster states surya's firmware knows?
found: Apparently not, for the two deepest. sm7150.dtsi (sm7150-mainline, the same in our tree) carries three cluster states whose latencies are surya's own but whose PSCI parameters are SC7180's: 0x41000044 (cluster power collapse), 0x41001244 and 0x4100b244. surya's own Android device tree (lpm-levels, cluster mode shifted by 4) has l3-pc 0x4, cx-off 0x224 and llcc-off 0xc24 - that is 0x41000044, 0x41002244 and 0x4100c244; 0x4100c244 is also what SM8150, the closest sibling, uses for its one cluster sleep. On the phone the deepest state (0x4100b244) was never entered once at runtime. Whether the firmware rejects, demotes or honours SC7180's values is not known: it is the first thing a measured suspend settles. SM7150 is not yet in mainline: the 2025 upstreaming series is to be resent, so a correction can go into it.
question: Does sm7150's device tree ask the firmware for the cluster states surya's firmware knows?

brief: Standby drain is made a repeatable test, scored as average current from the charge counter delta; no standard 'suitcase test' exists
found: Yes, repeatable - but scored as mean current, not battery percent. Observed (Android power-component guide, source.android.com/docs/core/power/component): measure suspend with no wakelocks, confirm the device really suspends, wait for the reading to settle, average radio current over time, unplug USB first (a host can feed current). GameBench: hourly drain = capacity / average current. No standard 'suitcase test' or 'overnight drain test' found; the name is ours. pmaports#4846 (motorola-dubai 17x Droidian; method unread). Droidian miatoll 9 mA: its method not found; PinePhone anecdotes are single reports. Inference: charge_counter delta over the whole window is the primary number, current_now only a cross-check (wake samples inflate it), the gauge percentage least trustworthy. Take: average over a window, a settle period, unplug before the run, proof of real suspend. Leave: percentage scoring, the 30-80 mA 'normal' figures, 6-8 h windows. Test-catalogue fit: test standby-current, threshold 15 mA, median of 3 runs, a witness step 'unplug USB, confirm'; one run row per attempt (start/end charge_counter, elapsed, mean mA, samples, suspended fraction, radio state, kernel, unplug time), a failed unplug is an invalid run not a zero. One-off run: >=60 min measured after a 10 min settle (10 min is too short, the counter is coarse); Wi-Fi on the lab AP, Bluetooth as two separate runs (on, off), SIM out so record the modem state and do not call it airplane mode; screen off; log current_now, charge_counter, voltage_now, status every 30-60 s with a monotonic time, plus wakeup and suspend counts; discard samples while status is Charging; score from the charge_counter delta, report suspended fraction, compare with 15 mA and 9 mA now, Android 'not known yet'.
question: Should standby drain be a proper repeatable test (idle, unplugged, fixed time, screen off, radios as in daily use) rather than a single measurement, and what should the one-off run prepared now take from it?

brief: Where does surya's deep sleep stand, measured on the phone itself?
found: Measured 2026-11-17 on the test kernel 7.1.0-rc3-sm7150-wcd, read only. The kernel offers only s2idle, as on every Qualcomm phone. PSCI 1.1 runs in OS-initiated mode, and the CPU and cluster idle states are in use at runtime. The SoC's own sleep counters are readable (qcom_stats, from rpmh-stats at 0xc3f0000). Since boot: no suspend at all (suspend_stats success 0 - on USB the lab holds devlab-usb, and Sxmo holds sxmo_not_suspendable and sxmo_modem_warming_up); CX collapse (cxsd) 0, AOSS sleep (aosd) 0, DDR low-power states 0; the deepest cluster state (cluster-sleep-2) never entered once while the lighter two were entered thousands of times. The audio DSP never slept (adsp 0) while the compute DSP and the modem slept about 200 times each; no audio stream was open, yet the VA, TX and RX macros stayed active, and the command line carries soundwire_qcom.stay_awake=1 from the microphone hunt. So no measurement of deep sleep exists yet, and two things already seen would keep the SoC from its floor.
question: Where does surya's deep sleep stand, measured on the phone itself?

brief: Why does the modem not go online once a SIM card is in?
found: With the SIM in (operator 1&1, card present and ready) the modem refuses every request to go online: its own operating mode reads shutting-down from the start of boot, and ModemManager gets DeviceNotReady. The modem processor boots cleanly; rmtfs and tqftpserv run; the kernel's pd-mapper module is loaded. Meanwhile the modem reads and writes /readwrite/lctoem.tmp over tqftpserv in an endless loop, with rsize=0 seek=0 options, each read ending at once - the same kind of loop that postmarketOS fixed for the Fairphone 4 and 5 with a tqftpserv that handles rsize and seek. A reboot with the SIM in place changed nothing.
question: Why does the modem not go online once a SIM card is in?

found: In stages, never at once. A first translator is written outside - in another language, as an interpreter, for a subset, or by hand - and needs only to be enough to carry the language's own saying of itself; that saying is then run through it, and then through itself, and the two results are compared: where they differ, one of them is wrong. So the outside is not thrown away when the inside can first speak; it stays beside it until the inside says the same, and what remains outside afterwards is small and is what touches the machine. For ocoeco this gives the order: move what is already declared (what an entry asks, how a row is named, where it is kept) before what acts on a surface (reading the words, writing the row); run the lens beside the program's saying and compare before taking the program's away - which is what was done for entering, tried as a place's own lens first; and keep the kernel that stays in the program small and named - the engine that answers queries, reading from surfaces, writing rows. What the comparison is for a compiler, a look kept before and compared after is here.
question: How did languages that were first said from outside - by assembly, by another language - come to say themselves, and what does that order teach for moving what the program says into the lenses?

found: Others who read a surface as a table agree on three things. The shape of a table is data: declared, not coded. The kinds of surface are few, and each is a small adapter in the program that makes rows when asked - nothing is stored. And which surface a table reads from is said beside its shape, the where a parameter. So here: a table's shape is said once - by the lens that defines it, else by the place's own declaration, else read off its rows; where its rows come from is a route, said in the language; and a table is entered as itself where no entry has its name. Three open things - a route said by a lens, a shape said where entries do not read, a next step that is words - were one question: what a table is, and where its rows come from.

found: Looked at ourselves first (2026-11-13). Of 36 parts in the lenses built in: 14 only filter the rows of one kind; 15 count or gather; 9 bring two kinds together; 8 take a name apart to find what it points at; 1 is placed. All 22 tables are declared as a minimum - a row may carry more - and all are keyed by id alone: they are kinds of thing with an id, not tables in the strict sense. And the work about what bears on what is done outside any table: 280 lines of the program check links, 473 rewrite them when rows move, 59 walk a chain. So tables serve us for counting and gathering, for a whole thing readable on one line, and for checks when written; they do not give identity, edges, walking, what points at a thing, or what was. In the world: a table is one way of sorting facts, not the facts - Datomic keeps facts and answers row-like and column-like questions from the same ones; identity can be what a thing is, with names as labels (Unison); a graph can be declared over tables that exist and walked in the engine we use (SQL/PGQ); and text at rest with a graph when asked is a working arrangement (Logseq), whose newer form warns against giving up the text. In power a table does nothing a graph of facts cannot; in practice it gives a mature, fast engine and a row a person can read whole. The middle man is at the asking, not at rest: at rest we already keep things with ids and links - nodes and edges, written as text.
question: How do tables serve the commons today, do they do something a graph of the best kind cannot, and how has the world dealt with what we are dealing with?

KNOWLEDGE - best: every claim with its source, and a question before an answer. Keeps: research, sources, concepts, vocabulary. Lacks: how a finding is known - measured, read, or reasoned; on 2026-11-12 a reasoned guess (a request with no time limit) stood beside measured facts and was wrong. REASONING - best: a decision on one page with its context, what was rejected, its consequences and its status (Toyota's A3, Nygard's decision records). Keeps: decisions with why, rejected, research, sources. Lacks: the relation between decisions - one refining or replacing another is written as text today, three times on 2026-11-12. WORK - best: visible flow, pull, limits, ageing (Kanban, Reinertsen). Keeps: the backlog's flow, driver, next, since, waits_on; oco-agent's journal says what actually ran. Lacks: why this work - its link to the milestone or decision it serves. RESULTS - best: evidence that can be checked, not a claim. Keeps: glimpses, workings with evidence, gathered releases, activity and test runs. Lacks: evidence as a link to the thing that proves it. LOOKING BACK - best: the After Action Review, hansei. Keeps: reflections. Lacks: nothing essential. PROBLEMS - best: the andon - a problem visible the moment it happens, to everyone, until it is dealt with. Keeps: nothing of its own; attention is computed for the flow only. Lacks: the lens itself - 21 release runs failed unseen and a watcher was silent for a night on 2026-11-12. The largest gap. INVITATION - best: a need marked where it is, small and well-defined, fillable by whoever passes (Wikipedia's citation needed, good-first-issue labels, citizen science, device owners filling a support table). Keeps: nothing. Lacks: the entity - what is needed, of what kind (information, a test on a device, feedback), where, and how to give it. What open commons add to Toyota's room. THE SKY ITSELF - what makes lenses one dome: relations seen as connections, the story, and time. Keeps: about 860 links that resolve, the essence a star tells, and history in git. Lacks: the relations declared - the dome's continuity rests on them. So, in order: declare the relations (among them one decision refining another, and work serving a milestone); the problems lens; the invitation; how a finding is known and evidence that links; then lenses as data.
question: Lens by lens, what does the best of the world's experience say - stripped of ceremony - and what does ocoeco keep or lack for it?

found: The best of it is Toyota's obeya, the big room: begun on the Prius project because no single person held the knowledge the work needed, its walls showed purpose, plan, progress, problems and countermeasures together, so that anyone entering saw the whole and problems became visible. Around it: make things visible (mieruka), signal a problem at once (andon), go and see the real thing, pull work rather than push it, a decision on one page with its reasoning (A3), and look back (hansei). found: Two things share the name monad and neither is the passthrough lens. In Haskell a monad chains steps that each carry something extra; what composes lenses there is plainer - optics compose as functions, and the identity is the lens that passes everything. Leibniz's monad is a standpoint: a simple substance mirroring the whole from its point of view - nearest to a place one looks from. What the world found as the smallest whole set: the identity; three ways into a shape - one part of what is side by side (a lens), one case of what is one of several (a prism), each of many (a traversal); two ways to go together - one after another, and side by side; and two directions - get and put - held to a law, that what is put is what is then got. Shapes themselves are made of the same two: this and that, this or that - down to the bit, the smallest this-or-that. A region of bits (from, how many) is the simplest lens there is, and formats are declared so. Against ocoeco (2026-11-14): both ways of going together exist (a shape read across lenses; places). The identity does not: a table is kept as another kind of thing than a lens, though it is the passthrough of what a place keeps. A lens's two faces, glimpse and focus, are put and get, but their law is nowhere said - one sign of it shows by accident: a table nothing brings into focus. And a lens is still a bundle of four things - what data is, how it enters, what bears on what, what comes into focus - with how it is laid out mixed in. Parts that count or gather only read: through those nothing can be put, and that is as it should be.
question: Is there a sense in a monad in our ecosystem - can all lenses be expressed from a simplest, passthrough lens - and how does it fit with shapes coming down to bits?

found: The author, 2026-11-12: a lens propagates light, it lets it through; by itself it shows nothing - it is not a screen or a picture - and the word showing falls off the full picture, as if from another domain. In optics a lens is defined by this: it transmits light and brings it to a focus; a telescope's lens gathers a star's faint light and focuses it, so that a blur becomes something one can make out. So the second face of a lens is its focus, and the act is to focus. It is plain and can be guessed (focus the lens on a star); it says the true thing about the data - nothing is made, the same data is brought into focus; and it leaves the showing where it happens, on the fulldome. The whole then reads as one picture: a star gives off light, its data; a glimpse catches it where it is fresh; a lens lets it through and brings it into focus; the fulldome is where it is seen; to observe is to gather the light of many stars. Shine is no act of ocoeco: it is what a star does by working.
question: What does a lens do with what passes through it - what is its second face called?
